title: Nanemoset (Wading River Brook)
summary: Nanemoset is a recorded Indigenous brook name whose exact location remains uncertain. William Wallace Tooker tentatively associated it with Wading River or a tributary, drawing on a 1663 Setauket land agreement and related names in Brookhaven records.
map_geometry_source: approximate Wading River Brook / hamlet marker; Nanemoset location uncertain
history_title: A Brook Name in Colonial Boundary Records
history_content:
A 1663 agreement between Setauket inhabitants and Captain John Scott described land bounded on the east by Nanemoset Brook. Tooker quoted this passage from Benjamin F. Thompson’s history of Long Island, volume II, page 321. The name survives because colonial land transactions used Indigenous waterways as boundary landmarks.1

Why the location remains uncertain

Tooker noted that De Kay had placed Nanemoset in Southampton. He proposed a different identification: because Scott also conveyed land bounded by Quaconsit River, or Wading River, Nanemoset might refer to that stream or one of its tributaries. This was Tooker’s inference, not a demonstrated match to a particular modern brook.1

He compared the name with Nemaukak in the 1655 Brookhaven deed and interpreted the forms in relation to fishing. In his separate Nemaukak entry he again stated that the exact locality was unknown. The surviving spelling is evidence of an Indigenous place name, but its translation and modern placement need to be read with that uncertainty.2
translation_content:
Alternate and related forms include Nanemoset, Namoss-es-et, and Nemaukak. The forms are interpreted around the idea of a fish-place or at/about the fishing-place. Earlier placement by De Kay is uncertain when compared with the Brookhaven and Wading River evidence.

Why Place Names Matter

“Exploring the names and stories associated with a place can foster a deep sense of belonging and connection.”

— National Library of New Zealand, Understanding the Context — Place Names and Collective Stories (n.d.), A sense of place section
whereintheworld_content: The map gives approximate orientation near Wading River, NY. The historical evidence does not identify one modern tributary securely, so the point should not be read as the site of a documented fishing station, settlement, or trail.1
